Ornaments by Period

The same trill or small note means different things in Baroque, Classical, Romantic, 20th and 21st-century, and jazz scores. Hear each reading, with right and wrong interpretations for every period, how improvisation fits in then and now, and a flow chart for any ornament you meet.

An ornament sign is shorthand, and what it stands for has changed over 300 years. A small note before a main note, or a tr over it, can mean four or five different things depending on when and where the piece was written. Reading the sign isn’t enough. You have to know whose shorthand it is.

This page:

  1. sets the five idioms side by side on one small note and one trill,
  2. gives right and wrong readings for each period,
  3. explains where improvisation fits, then and now,
  4. ends with a flow chart that walks you from the ornament in front of you to a way to play it.

Press ▶ on any example to hear it. The notes shown are what is played, not just what is written.

One sign, five meanings

A small note before the main note

Every reading in the table below starts from the same written notes:

Idiom How it's played Played
Baroque
to c. 1750		 An appoggiatura: on the beat, leaning on the dissonance, long. Half of the main note is the default, more before a long note.
Classical
c. 1750–1820		 The same: on the beat and long, usually half (Leopold Mozart; Türk). Short graces before quick or repeated notes. Mozart often writes the long ones out in full-size notes.
Romantic
c. 1820–1900		 Mostly short. Chopin wants it on the beat, struck with the bass (Eigeldinger). Later in the century short graces often go before the beat (Brown).
20th and 21st century Before the beat, as quickly as possible, so the main note lands on the beat. Scores that want something else say so in a performance note (Gould).
Jazz and blues A smear: one note sliding into the next, before or across the beat. ▶ plays it as a slide on guitar.

The key line runs between Classical and Romantic. Before about 1820 the small note is a real note that takes the beat and much of the main note’s time. After that it’s usually a quick flick, and from the 20th century it goes before the beat.

A trill

Every reading starts from the same written trill:

Idiom How it's played Played
Baroque From the note above, on the beat, leaning on the first note. The trill is a decorated appoggiatura (J. S. Bach; C. P. E. Bach).
Classical Still from the note above, now even, often with a closing turn into the next note (Türk; Clementi).
Romantic From the main note: Hummel (1828) says the start from above "was made for the voice". Chopin too, unless he writes a small note before the trill (Hummel; Ekier).
20th and 21st century From the main note, unmeasured: as many notes as fit, as fast as possible. The speed, the note it trills with, even a slowing or speeding trill, may be written into the score (Gould).
Jazz A shake: a wide, loose lip trill (on trumpet, often a third or more), with no fixed number of notes (Pejrolo and DeRosa; Barnhart). ▶ plays it on guitar.

Baroque: the player finishes the music

A Baroque score is incomplete on purpose. Composers expected the player to add graces, and in France each composer printed a table of his own signs (d’Anglebert 1689, Couperin 1713). The defaults are clear: ornaments start on the beat, and from the note above (J. S. Bach; C. P. E. Bach). How many to add, and where, is taste. Some scholars argue that Bach’s trills could start on the main note too (Neumann, Ornamentation in Baroque). Most players today still start them from above.

Here is the opening of the Sarabande from Bach’s English Suite No. 3, as plain as Bach wrote it the first time. He then wrote out an ornamented version of his own (Les agréments de la même Sarabande).

Valid

French style: graces on the strong notes. An appoggiatura leans on beat 2, where a sarabande puts its weight. A trill from above goes on the leading tone, and a mordent on the last note. The tune stays the same.

Valid

Italian style: fill in the long notes. The long notes become running notes (passaggi, or divisions) that circle the written pitch. The notes on the beat are still Bach’s, so the harmony doesn’t change.

Not appropriate

Ornaments everywhere, and a trill on the resolution. A mordent on every note flattens the dance: beat 2 no longer stands out. The trill on the final G is the worst of it. A trill adds tension, so it belongs on the note before the resolution, never on the resolution itself.

Not appropriate

A 19th-century reading. The trill starts on the main note, and the grace on beat 2 is crushed into a flick before the beat. Both are right in Chopin. Here they lose the two dissonances, the leaning A against B♭ and the trill’s upper note, that the Baroque ornaments exist to make.

Classical: written down more, still on the beat

The rules hardly change from the late Baroque. Appoggiaturas fall on the beat and take half the main note, or two-thirds of a dotted one (Leopold Mozart; Türk; Clementi), and trills start from the note above. What changes is how much the composer writes. Mozart often writes his appoggiaturas as full-size notes and writes out the decorations of a slow movement, so there is less for the player to add (Neumann, Ornamentation and Improvisation in Mozart). There are still two places to improvise: the cadenza at the fermata in a concerto, and the short Eingang (lead-in) at a pause before a theme comes back.

The phrase below is written for this page in the Classical style.

Valid

The textbook reading. Each appoggiatura takes half its note, on the beat. The short grace before the quick F is short, and the trill starts from above and ends on a quick anticipation of the last note.

Valid

On the repeat, a little more. A turn fills the first bar and a rising figure leads into the third. Every decoration starts and ends on the written notes. This is what Mozart writes out himself when a melody comes back.

Not appropriate

Crushed graces and a main-note trill. Every appoggiatura is flicked away, so the sighs (D against C, A against G) disappear. Leopold Mozart and Türk both treat the long appoggiatura as the expressive heart of the phrase. The trill from the main note is the 19th-century habit.

Romantic: short, and the composer decides

Through the 19th century grace notes get shorter and move towards (or before) the beat, and trills start on the main note (Brown; Hummel). Composers write ever more precisely what they want, and the player’s job shifts from adding ornaments to shaping the ones written. Chopin is the famous exception: grace notes and trills start with the bass note, on the beat (Eigeldinger; Ekier).

Valid (Chopin)

With the bass. The grace note sounds together with the low E♭, as a quick lean, and the trill starts on its main note F.

Valid (later 19th century)

Before the beat. In much later Romantic music (and in Chopin’s early Contredanse, by his editors’ reading) the grace goes before the beat, so the bass and the main note sound together (Brown; Ekier).

Not appropriate

A Baroque appoggiatura. A long lean on C takes half the beat and smothers the melody’s first note. The trill starts from above, and an extra turn is added. None of it was asked for: by now the composer writes what he wants.

20th and 21st century: read the legend

Concert music after about 1900 mostly writes out exactly what it wants. Where signs survive, the general conventions are: grace notes before the beat, trills from the main note and as fast as possible, and nothing added (Gould). Many scores invent their own signs, for microtones, trills that speed up or slow down, or extended techniques, and explain them in a performance note at the front. That note overrules any period rule. Improvisation returns in a new form: some scores give a box of notes to repeat freely, or a graphic to interpret, and say so.

Valid

The default. The grace goes before the beat, and the trill is unmeasured from the main note.

Valid, if the legend says so

On the beat. Some composers ask for graces on the beat. If the performance note says so, that’s the right reading, and only then.

Not appropriate

A Baroque reading. A long appoggiatura on the beat and a trill from above would be right in Bach. Here they change the composer’s rhythm and harmony.

Jazz: the player owns the sound

In jazz the written notes are an outline. Grace notes, falls and scoops are part of a player’s sound: they come before or across the beat, in swing time, and are mostly not written at all (Caniato). A big-band chart writes them as signs (fall, doit, scoop, plop, shake), and the section plays them the way its lead player does. Singers and soloists add them freely. ▶ plays the slides on a clean electric guitar, so a fall really falls.

Valid

A fall off the long note. The line is swung, and the last note falls away at its release, never before the beat.

Valid

Scoop in, shake out. The first note slides up from below, and the long note gets a shake after it has sounded straight for a moment. That’s Armstrong’s “terminal vibrato” made wider (Schuller).

Not appropriate

A Classical trill, played straight. Even eighths and a measured trill from above, closed with a neat turn. Every note is “right”, but the line no longer swings, and a jazz shake is looser and wider than this.

Improvisation, then and now

Ornaments are what remains in the notation of a much larger habit of making music up on the spot. How much of that habit a score expects changes from period to period:

Period What the player was expected to invent Today
Baroque Graces on almost any note; divisions on slow movements, above all on the repeat; the chords over a figured bass; cadenzas at fermatas (C. P. E. Bach; Quantz) Early-music players add their own again. Bach’s written-out agréments and ornamented editions of Corelli’s slow movements are the models.
Classical Cadenzas in concertos, Eingänge at pauses, decoration of repeats in slow movements and arias (Neumann, Ornamentation and Improvisation in Mozart) Players play written cadenzas (Mozart’s own, Beethoven’s) or write their own; singers decorate the repeats in Mozart’s arias.
Romantic Less and less: composers write the ornaments and the cadenzas themselves Play what’s written. Shape the written ornaments with rubato and tone instead of adding to them.
20th and 21st century Nothing, unless the score asks. Then sometimes a great deal: free repetition, graphic scores, open form. Follow the performance note.
Jazz Almost everything: the melody’s shape, the ornaments, the solo The heart of the style. The written melody is a starting point.

Two things hold across all of them:

  • Ornaments serve the structure. Baroque, Classical and jazz improvisers all decorate weak notes and long notes, and leave the arrivals (cadences, downbeats, chord tones) clear.
  • More isn’t better. C. P. E. Bach compared too many ornaments to too much seasoning (C. P. E. Bach, ch. 2). A Basie section player would say much the same about a fall on every note.

Which way do I play it?

Pick the period, or type a composer, and answer the questions. Each step stays on the chart, so you can change an answer and see where the path goes instead.
